condition: Unsafe/premature discharge — impaired discharge readiness in acute decompensated heart failure, evidenced by unresolved exertional hypoxemia plus knowledge, financial, and home-environment barriers placing the client at high risk for decompensation and 30-day readmission
evaluationParameters: Repeat ambulation/exertion tolerance: SpO2 maintained at or above 90% on room air while walking a comparable distance, with no supplemental oxygen required for recovery, and no dyspnea, chest pain, or abnormal heart rate/blood pressure response

Documented discharge-readiness endpoints: successful teach-back of new medications, daily weight monitoring, and HF warning signs (weight gain >2-3 lb/day or >5 lb/week, increasing dyspnea, edema), plus confirmed possession of an affordable diuretic, a home scale, and an arranged follow-up/home support plan
missingInformation: Resting room-air SpO2 and whether the client has a baseline or home oxygen requirement
Vital signs, heart rate/blood pressure response, respiratory rate, and symptoms recorded during and after the 40-foot walk, and the liter flow/duration of oxygen needed to recover
Lung sounds, jugular venous distension, and peripheral edema on current assessment
Actual serial weights, admission-to-current weight change, and net intake/output
Specific BNP values and trend, plus renal function, electrolytes (especially potassium), and hemoglobin
Ejection fraction and HF type (HFrEF vs HFpEF) and the specific new medication regimen prescribed
Insurance/prescription coverage, exact out-of-pocket cost of the diuretic, and availability of formulary alternatives or assistance programs
Cognitive/health-literacy screening results, vision and hearing status, and any language barrier affecting teach-back
Availability of family, neighbors, or caregivers for support, transportation, and stair assistance
Fall risk and functional mobility assessment relevant to a second-floor walk-up (ability to climb stairs safely)
Whether home health, cardiac rehabilitation, telehealth monitoring, or a case management/social work consult has already been requested
Number and timing of prior HF admissions and scheduled follow-up appointment date
priorityActions: Hold/delay the 11:00 discharge and immediately notify the provider of the exertional desaturation to 89% requiring supplemental oxygen, requesting reassessment of discharge readiness and orders for continued oxygen saturation monitoring and activity evaluation; keep the client on prescribed oxygen with activity in the interim

Initiate coordinated discharge planning now — consult case management/social work and pharmacy for medication affordability (assistance program or an affordable formulary alternative) and for a home scale, arrange home health/support given she lives alone in a second-floor walk-up, and repeat structured teach-back education on medications, daily weights, and HF warning signs until she demonstrates understanding
reasoning: Although the objective HF markers (BNP and weight) are improving, the client demonstrates two independent, unresolved discharge barriers. Physiologically, desaturation to 89% after only 40 feet with an oxygen requirement to recover shows she has not achieved the functional/oxygenation stability needed to live alone and climb stairs to a second-floor apartment; this is the acute safety issue and must be communicated to the provider before the 11:00 discharge proceeds. Psychosocially, failed teach-back, inability to afford the prescribed diuretic, and absence of a home scale mean the self-management plan that prevents re-decompensation cannot be executed at home — the classic drivers of early HF readmission. The unifying condition is therefore not recurrent fluid overload but unsafe/premature discharge with impaired discharge readiness. The two priority actions address the physiologic barrier (stop the clock, escalate to the provider, continue oxygen monitoring with activity) and the resource/knowledge barriers (interdisciplinary referral for affordability, scale, home support, and repeat teach-back). Evaluation logically mirrors those actions: repeat exertional oximetry demonstrating SpO2 at least 90% on room air without oxygen, and objective confirmation that teach-back is passed and the medication, scale, and support resources are actually in place.
